name: Albin Countergambit
subtitle: Answer a wing offer with a central wedge.

ideas.idea: Challenge White's centre immediately instead of patiently defending it. If White captures, an advanced d-pawn can gain space, obstruct development, and make ordinary-looking moves uncomfortable. Your compensation relies on active pieces supporting that wedge.
ideas.structure: The advanced d-pawn is both an asset and a potential target. It restricts White, but it can become isolated if you fail to develop. White may keep the extra e-pawn, give it back to finish development, or attack your centre from the sides.
ideas.pieces: Develop the queen-side knight and bishops actively, with pressure toward the centre and White's king. The light-squared bishop can use an open diagonal; decide where your king belongs from the concrete position rather than assuming opposite-side castling is mandatory.
ideas.motifs: A pawn near the enemy back rank creates unusual tactical possibilities. In the Lasker-trap family, a bishop check and an underpromotion can exploit careless development; this is a warning to calculate, not a guarantee that White will cooperate. Also watch pins and attacks against a king still in the centre.
ideas.declined: If White does not take, resolve the central tension on its merits and develop. You may get a normal material balance with active central play. Do not push an unsupported pawn just to imitate the accepted variation.
ideas.caution: White has sound ways to return material, blockade the wedge, and complete development. If your activity runs out, reassess the pawn structure instead of searching indefinitely for a trap.

modelGames.summary: Black uses the d4 wedge to cramp White, attacks with the h-pawn and takes over the light squares. When White's pieces drift, Black's knights invade and the d-pawn becomes a monster.

moments.title: The d4 wedge
moments.note: Black's pawn on d4 takes away natural squares from White's knights and makes e3 harder to play. This space advantage is Black's main compensation.

moments.title: The h-pawn attack
moments.note: ...h5 heads for h4 to open the h-file toward White's fianchettoed king. A rook behind the pawn turns the open file into an attacking lane.

moments.title: A knight on b3
moments.note: The knight lands on b3, a hole fixed by the a4 pawn. It attacks the rook on a1 and keeps White tied up on the queenside.

moments.title: Pawn back, king exposed
moments.note: Black regains the pawn on c4 with check. White's king stays in the centre, and Black's queen is very active.

moments.title: A deflection
moments.note: The knight sacrifice on f2 pulls the queen away from defending d1. Active pieces create tactics like this.

moments.title: Material and the open file
moments.note: Black ends up ahead in material and takes the h-file. The d-pawn, which started as a wedge, is now a passed pawn near promotion.

modelGames.summary: White fianchettoes, targets the d4 pawn and ruins Black's kingside structure. Black's activity runs out, the wedge falls and White's extra pawns win the endgame.

moments.title: The long diagonal
moments.note: White's bishop on g2 points at b7 and supports a later attack on d4. The fianchetto is a reliable way to blunt the Albin's piece play.

moments.title: Target the wedge
moments.note: Both knights now eye d4. Once that pawn falls, Black's main compensation disappears.

moments.title: A broken kingside
moments.note: White exchanged bishop for knight to wreck Black's pawns. The doubled f-pawns and weak h7 give White long-term targets.

moments.title: The d4 pawn falls
moments.note: White wins the d4 pawn. Black has some activity left, but White has an extra pawn and the better structure.

moments.title: A runaway h-pawn
moments.note: White's passed h-pawn advances and draws Black's king to the corner. Passed pawns stretch the defence in the endgame.

moments.title: Defence complete
moments.note: White's king walks forward and the extra material wins. In the Albin, the defender's plan is to win the d4 pawn and survive to the endgame.
